claim: Statement line placement or blank lines change codegen.
source: general decomp folklore
evidence: The reference repo ran the control: this project builds without -g, so inserting blank lines anywhere yields a byte-identical object. Workbench levers 23/25/33 state that uopt/ugen honor statement line boundaries even at -g0, and that cfe numbers statements by LOGICAL line -- so splicing two statements onto ONE physical line makes them tie on lineno and lets ready-list position decide the schedule. claim: A permuter output directory named `output-100...` proves a byte-exact match.
source: own implementation, caught by external review
evidence: solver/pipeline.py::run_permuter parses a score from a DIRECTORY NAME and sets exact=True at >=100 without the oracle ever confirming it. This violates the project's foundational invariant -- byte-exact object comparison is the only source of truth. A false EXACT is worse than a missed match: it poisons every downstream number and the ratchet would lock it in. Every permuter result must be re-scored through workspace.score() and judged on 'Verified exact match'. SEVERITY WAS UNDERSTATED. Measured directly: permuter output directories are named by dist.py COST (lower is better), not by a percentage. output-3750 scores 17.98% through the oracle; output-3700 scores 21.83%; output-35 scores 99.36%. The old code read the directory number as a percentage and set exact=True at >=100, so nearly EVERY permuter output would have been declared a byte-exact match -- a 17.98% candidate included. It never fired only because no function in any completed run took the permute route. That is luck, not safety.
tested_on: code inspection, verified

claim: Supplying verified type facts (array stride, narrow parameter widths, frame size, KB access widths) will let the solver match medium and larger functions.
source: the premise behind six loop iterations of prompt enrichment
evidence: With the hints live for the first time, medium-tier mean went 49.8 -> 48.3 and exact stayed at 0. The routing shows why: ALL 10 medium and ALL 9 large functions routed to `reshape`, and not one reached `retype`, `permute` or `relocation`. Medium scores run 0-96%, mostly 27-55%. These are not near-misses with wrong types -- they are structurally wrong programs. Every type hint built targets the retype band, which medium functions do not reach, so the hints were aimed at a failure mode that is not occurring there. They did move `small` (79.5 -> 90.7, the only tier delta all night to clear the +/-10 noise floor), which is consistent: small functions DO sometimes reach retype.
tested_on: v3 dev run, 39/87 partial, paired against the pre-fix run

claim: The wall above `small` is structural -- wrong control flow and program shape -- not missing type information.
source: route distribution in the v3 run
evidence: CONFIRMED decisively, with zero GPU, by diagnosing objects already on disk from the v3 run. 30 of the 39 hard functions had usable candidates: 29 returned structure-mismatch (96.7%), 1 returned no verdict. Zero returned allocation, constant, frame-layout, schedule or relocation. By tier: medium 16/16, large 10/10, huge 3/3. Independently, 27 of 29 differ from the target in INSTRUCTION COUNT, which is structural by definition -- register allocation cannot change how many instructions exist. The earlier ambiguity is resolved: `reshape` was not merely the score<80 fallback, the workbench genuinely classifies these as structural. CONSEQUENCE: the wall is the model emitting a differently-shaped program, not missing facts about types. That explains every null result -- type hints, base resolution and the permuter all address non-structural residuals. The remaining levers are structural: sibling mirroring, decomposition, or model capability.
tested_on: 30 hard functions diagnosed from existing v3 objects

claim: Leaf functions are easier to match than non-leaf ones, so the eval set should stratify on it.
source: own assumption when designing eval/sets.py
evidence: Measured over 68 completed functions: leaf 27.8% exact, non-leaf 28.1%. No difference whatsoever. Non-leaf functions actually have a HIGHER mean score (77.1 vs 62.2). Call count is not monotonic either -- functions with 1-4 calls match BEST (38.9%), better than functions with none. Inter-function context is not the difficulty. Half the eval stratification was spent on a non-factor.
tested_on: v3 dev run, 68 functions

claim: Match probability is governed by function size and memory-access density, with hard cliffs rather than a gradient.
source: predictor analysis of the v3 run
evidence: 68 functions. By instruction count: 71.4% / 15.0% / 5.9% / 0.0% across <20, 20-50, 50-120, 120+. By memory accesses: 66.7% / 28.0% / 0.0% / 0.0% across <5, 5-15, 15-40, 40+. TWO HARD CLIFFS: above 15 memory accesses, 0 of 25 matched; above 5 unknown-base accesses, 0 of 25 matched. These are not 'harder' regions, they are zero. Tier labels (tiny/small/medium/large) are just a proxy for instruction count.
tested_on: v3 dev run, 68 functions across 4 size tiers

claim: Improving the evidence tier's base resolution (currently 58.4%) would raise the match rate, because functions whose bases the KB cannot resolve are exactly the ones that fail.
source: predictor analysis
evidence: REFUTED by the controlled test its own entry specified. Holding function size constant and splitting each band at its median unknown-base count: 0-20 insns low 62% vs high 88% (REVERSED), 20-50 low 20% vs high 11%, 50-120 low 9% vs high 0%, 120+ both 0%. The unknown/mem RATIO is non-monotonic across all sizes: 35%, 9%, 12%, 31%. The raw correlation was function size in disguise. CONSEQUENCE: improving the evidence tier's 58.4% base resolution would NOT raise the match rate, so dataflow analysis to resolve more bases is not the lever. Caveat: cells hold 4-13 functions, so this is suggestive rather than definitive -- but the reversal in the smallest band and the non-monotonic ratio both argue against a real effect. Mean scores do fall slightly with high unknown counts within bands; exact rate, which is what counts, does not.
tested_on: v3 run, 71 attempted functions, within-band split

claim: A function that errors during setup can be recorded at 0% alongside genuine model failures without distorting the result.
source: user asked whether an internet outage had corrupted the run
evidence: Two v3 functions were logged 0.00% with draws=0 and wall=0s -- no model call ever happened. They were request timeouts, recorded identically to functions the solver genuinely failed. Impact on the run: exact 27.5% -> 28.4%, mean 68.2% -> 70.2% once excluded. CAUSE: --timeout was lowered 900s -> 300s for v3 to bound a hung request, which converted two intermittently-slow calls into recorded failures; every earlier run used 900s and is clean. Ollama demonstrably stalls at times -- a 5-token prompt was measured at 76s. run_set now reports never-ran rows separately and excludes them from rates and means. Not caused by the network outage: the later of the two rows was written after connectivity returned.
tested_on: v3 dev run, 69 rows; audit of all 5 prior result files

claim: The correctness and routing work (hints wired in, verdict-first routing, oracle-verified permuting, adaptive context) raises the match rate.
source: an evening of fixes following external review
evidence: v3 dev run, 87 functions, first result with a config fingerprint. 84 attempted: 19 exact (22.6%), mean 60.9%. PAIRED against the pre-fix run on 65 shared functions: exact 19 -> 18, mean 69.75 -> 69.49. Both deltas sit well inside the measured noise floor (exact <3, mean <10), so the honest reading is NO CHANGE. By tier: tiny 71.4%, small 15.8%, medium 5.3%, large 0/15, huge 0/10 (first ever attempted, mean 9.6%). One match in 44 functions above `small`. The fixes remain correct and worth keeping -- run_permuter could fabricate an EXACT from a directory name, and the ratchet would have locked it in -- but correctness is not measured in score. They make the number trustworthy, not higher.
tested_on: v3 dev, 87 functions, fingerprinted, paired on 65

claim: A candidate scoring >=95% has a register-allocation residual, so the permuter can close it.
source: the original score-band triage design
evidence: All three >=95% functions in the hard subset were routed to `reshape`, not `permute` -- and that is informative, because with an empty verdict the >=95% band falls back to permute. Getting reshape proves the workbench returned a STRUCTURAL verdict despite the high score. Tested directly on isRacePlayerRespawnSurfaceValid (95.77%): 400s of permuting produced 19 candidates, best oracle-verified 99.36%, no match. Prediction stated before the run and held. A high score does not imply the residual is allocation, which is exactly why routing on score alone was wrong.
tested_on: 3 near-misses routed; 1 permuted for 400s, 19 candidates verified

claim: A substantial share of large/huge-function generations are refusals recorded as failures, so those tiers' numbers are contaminated.
source: inspecting why huge-tier candidates were 5-instruction stubs
evidence: 96 of 694 candidate files (13.8%) contain refusal text. By tier: tiny 0/98 candidates, small 0/135, medium 11/123 (9%), large 47/96 (49%), huge 30/60 (50%). 87% of large functions and 80% of huge ones had at least one refused generation. The refusal rate tracks the performance collapse exactly. Best-of-3 with a 50% refusal rate is effectively best-of-1.5, so the large (0/15) and huge (0/10) results measure a model that declined half the attempts. Refusals also emit ~5-instruction stubs, which diagnose as structure-mismatch -- partially contaminating that finding for large/huge, though medium (9% refusals) stands. CORRECTION, from a follow-up check of my own claim: saying these tiers 'measure a model that declined half the attempts' OVERSTATED the contamination. best_score is a MAX across candidates and a refusal scores ~0, so a max ignores refusals. Measured directly: ZERO functions had no usable candidate -- every one got at least one genuine attempt, so the recorded scores stand. The real effect is UNDER-SAMPLING: usable draws were 100% for tiny/small, 91% medium, 52% large, 47% huge. Large and huge got about half the effective best-of-N. That does not rescue their results: tiny reaches 71% on ~4.7 usable draws while large gets 0% on ~3.3, and a 2x sampling deficit cannot produce a 71-point gap. Size remains the dominant factor; the refusals make those tiers under-sampled, not fabricated.
tested_on: 694 candidate files across the v3 run

claim: The refusals are triggered by 'You are decompiling a Nintendo 64 game' and will stop if the task is reframed as compiler-output reconstruction.
source: the obvious reading of the refusal text
evidence: Reframed the prompt to drop all game/decompilation framing and retested on two previously-refusing functions. The model still refused, adapting its wording to the new framing ('I can't provide the solution to this challenge', 'I can't produce the requested source'), and one variant wrote prose claiming the function was 'not recoverable from the given assembly dump'. Prediction was stated before the test and FAILED. This is capability capitulation wearing refusal language, not a safety refusal. Consequence: a prompt fix cannot recover the large/huge tiers; it needs a model that does not bail, or a task decomposed small enough that it does not want to.
tested_on: 2 previously-refusing functions, reframed prompt, n=2 each

claim: gpt-oss:20b's refusals on large/huge functions are costing matches; a model that attempts them would do better.
source: the natural reading of the refusal finding
evidence: Tested directly on three functions gpt-oss refused: ran qwen2.5-coder:14b, which produced NINE genuine attempts and zero refusals, up to 20KB of C per attempt. Scores: 0.00%, 0.87%, 0.00%. Attempting is worth no more than declining on these functions. Prediction stated beforehand -- qwen refuses less but scores no better -- and BOTH halves held. CONSEQUENCE: the refusals were a symptom, not a cause. Removing them recovers nothing, so the large/huge tiers are genuinely beyond both local models: one declines, the other emits confidently wrong code, and the outcome is identical.
tested_on: 3 large/huge functions, qwen2.5-coder:14b, 9 attempts

claim: Splitting the READING of a long function across fresh instances, each seeing a bounded region, eliminates the refusals that appear only on long functions.
source: user's proposal: shifts and breaks, do not topple one instance
evidence: REPLICATED on 3 functions: drawMenuAsciiFontTile (182 lines, 4 regions), getRacePlayerRankingProgress (345, 8), checkMainMenuSecretCode (265, 6). 18 of 18 region reads succeeded, ZERO refusals -- against a baseline where these same functions refuse ~50% of the time when read whole (and where the composer, given the whole thing, refused 5 of 6 draws in the same run). Same model, same day, same flags: the only variable is how much it is asked to hold. This is now the only surviving explanation for the refusals -- copyright framing and capability capitulation are both REFUTED. SCOPE: this confirms bounded-region READING does not refuse. It does NOT claim regions produce matches; see the composer results, which are separate and much weaker. FURTHER REPLICATION (2026-08-28, entry 0): 27 more region reads across 6 functions, again ZERO refusals -- 45 of 45 region reads across 9 functions now. In the same run the composers, given those same functions whole, refused 9 of 36 draws. The region finding is unaffected by the compression result being killed: they are separate claims, and only the second failed. REPORTING CORRECTION (external review): excluding refusals from failure statistics is correct when measuring MODEL CAPABILITY, but wrong when measuring END-TO-END SYSTEM SUCCESS -- for an automated decompiler, a refusal is a failed attempt regardless of why. Both denominators must be reported side by side from now on. Past numbers quoting only the capability denominator flatter the system. FINAL SCOPE (2026-08-28): bounded reading eliminates refusals completely and reliably -- 45/45 region reads, 0/54 slices. But entry 2 showed that eliminating every refusal produces zero additional matches. The finding is real and narrow: it changes model BEHAVIOUR, not matching ability. It should not be cited as progress toward byte-exact reconstruction.
tested_on: 9 functions, 45 region reads, 0 refusals (2026-08-28)

claim: A composer can write byte-exact C from region SUMMARIES alone, without the full assembly.
source: the obvious way to unload the composition step
evidence: Tested directly as arm B (summaries + lexicon, NO assembly) against arm C (summaries + lexicon + stripped assembly), same shared summaries, 6 draws each. B and C compiled equally often (2 of 6), but scored 0.8 vs 20.0 summed-best. Removing the assembly did not stop the composer refusing (3 of 6 either way) and cost nearly all of the score. So the detail cannot simply be dropped: a summary-only composer produces code that compiles and is wrong. The lexicon is a SUPPLEMENT to the assembly, not a replacement for it. Composition must stay grounded in the instructions.
tested_on: 3 functions, 6 draws per arm (2026-08-28)

claim: Stripping the /* offset vram encoding */ comments and attaching a lexicon of exact facts cuts the composer's input to ~34% and lets it attempt functions it otherwise refuses.
source: user's proposal: compress, plus a lexicon to check against, so it is lookup and not entire retrieval
evidence: KILLED by its own pre-registered kill condition at n=18 per arm (6 functions x 3 draws, stratified medium/large/huge). Refusals: A raw 4/18 (22%), C lexicon+stripped 5/18 (28%). The gap is -1 -- compression refused MORE. The condition was 'gap <= 1 means dead', and it is dead. Scores over compiled candidates: A mean 38.9 / median 29.7 (n=4), C mean 20.5 / median 17.7 (n=6). C compiled slightly more often (6 vs 4) but scored lower. Every one of those differences is below the significance floor, so the honest summary is NO EFFECT, with weak evidence of harm. The n=6 result that motivated this was noise, as flagged when it was recorded: arm A's 5/6 refusal rate there is 4/18 here. This is exactly why entry 0 existed and why nothing was built on it. CONSEQUENCE: strip_asm and lexicon() stay in the tree -- they are correct, validated at 82/82 globals, and lossless -- but they do NOT become the default composer path. A hypothesis does not get to change behaviour. NOTE the one striking datum, from the RAW arm: checkMainMenuSecretCode draw 1 scored 90.8%, the highest score this project has produced. Worth chasing on its own; it is not evidence for either arm. CAVEAT: two arm-A draws on drawPulsingAssetTableSprite returned in 0s and were counted 'no compile'. A 0s generation is almost certainly a degenerate empty response, so arm A's no-compile count is if anything flattered -- which does not change the verdict, since arm A already won.
tested_on: 6 functions x 3 draws x 2 arms, n=18 per arm (2026-08-28)

claim: Slices should emit C and carry forward the declarations made by earlier slices (WaDec 'temporal context'), instead of emitting prose summaries that one composer reads in a single shot.
source: WaDec, ICSE 2025 (arXiv 2406.11346), 52.11% recompilability
evidence: Built and tested on 6 functions x 2 draws, paired against entry 0 arm A on the SAME functions. Clean run: 0 of 54 slices refused, 0 truncated, 1 of 54 empty. THE MECHANISM WORKS. claim: Prefill caused the lost exact match by dropping struct padding.
source: diffing the lost exact match against its prefilled replacement
evidence: isRacePlayerRespawnSurfaceValid went 100.00 EXACT -> 91.75 under prefill. Diffing the two stored candidates shows exactly one substantive difference. The exact version padded: 'u8 _pad0[0x1C]; int field1; u8 _pad1[0x24-0x20]; int field2; u8 _pad2[0x502-0x28]; s16 surfaceId;'. The prefilled version wrote 's32 field1C; s32 field24; s16 field502;' with NO padding at all, so those fields sit at 0, 4 and 8 instead of 0x1C, 0x24 and 0x502. Likely mechanism: the exact candidate is 1643 chars with explanatory comments reasoning about each padding gap; the prefilled one is 946 chars and terse. Starting the reply mid-code appears to skip the deliberation that produced the padding, not just the preamble. That is a real cost of prefill and it is invisible in aggregate scores. DIRECTLY FIXABLE: structgen.repad() exists for exactly this, and the field names encode their own offsets (field1C, field24, field502), which is the signal repad uses to place them. Prefill for reach plus repad for correctness is the obvious pairing. Also noted: prefill supplies '#include "common.h"' and the model writes it again, so every prefilled candidate carries a duplicate include. Harmless under include guards, but sloppy and worth trimming. ||| REFUTED (2026-08-29). I diagnosed this from a SOURCE diff and never checked the INSTRUCTION diff. Padding was the most visible difference and not the operative one. repad was extended to INSERT padding (a real gap it had), applied cleanly, and the score did not move: 91.750 -> 91.750. Narrowing the callee's first parameter to s16 moved it 0.058, to 91.808. The actual instruction diff shows something else entirely: target 'lw a1,0x1c(a3); lw a2,0x24(a3); lh a0,0x502(a0)' versus candidate 'lw a1,0x24(a3); lh a2,0x502(a3); lh a0,0x1e(a0)'. The candidate passes the WRONG STRUCT FIELDS to the callee -- a different argument mapping, which is ordinary model error, not a formatting artifact. Second difference: 'li v1,1 ... move v0,v1' against the target's direct 'li v0,1', caused by an extra local variable. My s16 signature change also made things worse in a way worth recording: 'lh a0,0x1e' reads the LOW HALF of the four-byte field at 0x1C, because MIPS is big-endian. I introduced that. So the lost exact match is SAMPLING VARIANCE -- a different, wrong reconstruction on this draw -- not a systematic prefill defect. Prefill does write terser structs, which is real, but it is not what cost the match. Lesson: the source diff and the instruction diff answer different questions, and only the second one says what the compiler saw. I made a confident causal claim from the first.

claim: A choice that is ambiguous inside one function is determined by how the rest of the program uses the same symbol.
source: user: this uses this register because another function uses it here
evidence: Built solver/callsig.py: for a given callee, scan every call site in the FULL program disassembly and aggregate what each argument register was last set from. Evidence-only -- disassembly, never source -- so it is usable on held-out functions and cannot leak ground truth. VALIDATED AGAINST GROUND TRUTH, 3 of 4 correct: addRenderCallback derived (pointer, pointer, passthrough) from 361 sites at 98-99% agreement, actual (RenderCallbackNode**, RenderCallback, void*). setCallbackTaskCallback derived a1=pointer at 203 of 204 sites, actual (void*, CallbackTaskCallback). removeCallbackTask a0=passthrough, actual (void*). THE FOURTH IS A CONCEPTUAL CORRECTION, not noise. getRaceCourseSurfaceType derived a0=s16; it is declared (s32, s32, s32). Both are true: the caller loads arg0 with `lh` and passes it sign-extended. This pass measures WHAT THE CALLER LOADS, not what the callee declares. For generating matching C that is the more useful fact -- the model must emit code that produces an lh -- but calling it a prototype would be wrong, and the docstring now says so. A PLUMBING BUG worth keeping: the first version read nonmatchings/<fn>/target.s and found 2 call sites for a function with 586 callers, because only ~91 functions have workspaces. Every widely-called symbol reported 'nothing confident' -- an empty result that looked like a weak signal rather than a broken scan. Reading repo/asm (2,306 files) gives 205-361 sites. A CLASSIFICATION BUG too: move/or/addiu were all lumped as unknown, so pointer arguments -- which is what utility functions mostly take -- were discarded as absent. Distinguishing pointer / passthrough / const / computed is what made the signal appear.

claim: A debugger-style symbolic trace -- what each register HOLDS rather than what each instruction does -- states outright the facts that take hours to reconstruct from raw assembly.
source: user: what if we made our own debugger with visible register values
evidence: solver/symtrace.py walks a function maintaining a symbolic expression per register. Deterministic, evidence-only, no model, safe on held-out functions. THE VALIDATION IS DIRECT. The first line of the trace for isRacePlayerRespawnSurfaceValid is 'CALL getRaceCourseSurfaceType(param0->f502, param0->f1c, param0->f24)'. That is the exact fact I failed to find with THREE wrong hypotheses -- struct padding, callee signature, argument order -- each moving the score by a fraction of a point because the real answer was a conjunction. The trace prints it. On updateTimeTrialRecordDeltaPopupSlideIn it produces 'param0->f1c = subu(param0->f1c, param0->f28)', 'param0->f18 = 0x5A', and 'CALL addRenderCallback(&gRaceOverlayRenderCallbackList, &drawTimeTrialRecordDeltaPopup, stack[0x18])' -- matching the real source line for line. THREE BUGS FOUND BY CHECKING RATHER THAN TRUSTING: sp was rewritten as a struct base so frame stores read as field accesses; an untouched a3 printed as a real fourth argument; and `lui` stashed a pending %hi that was never committed, so a global address passed via lui alone -- which happens whenever the symbol's low half is zero -- was reported as param0. That last one made addRenderCallback's first argument silently wrong. SCOPE: straight-line symbolic execution. Branches are noted, not explored; arithmetic is not evaluated to concrete values; trailing argument registers are dropped rather than guessed, because a scratch copy like `move a3,a0` is indistinguishable from a fourth argument from inside the function. A reading aid, not an emulator.

claim: The symbolic trace states the call arguments, so they can be written into a candidate mechanically -- no model, oracle-verified, the same shape as repad.
source: user: an A/B here would be a bit of a false dichotomy
evidence: THE FRAMING IS RIGHT and worth keeping regardless of this implementation. Measuring the trace by asking 'does the model do better with it in the prompt' would have been the EIGHTH prompt-content experiment after seven nulls, and it would have tested the weakest use. The trace does not hint at the call, it states it. solver/tracefix.py attempts the mechanical rewrite and DOES NOT WORK YET. It produces the correct argument list -- '(player->field502, player->field1C, player->field24)', exactly the answer -- but writes it into the wrong place and the result does not compile. FOUR BUGS IN SUCCESSION, and the pattern in them is the finding: (1) `f(void)` treated as a one-argument call, so it INVENTED a parameter; (2) trailing scratch-copy argument not dropped; (3) field-name offset parsed as 0xd502 instead of 0x502, because the 'd' of 'field' is a hex digit -- repad already solves this by disambiguating against observed offsets and the solution was not carried across; (4) the rewrite lands on the extern PROTOTYPE rather than the call site -- argperm hit and fixed this exact bug an hour earlier, also not carried across. Two of four are bugs already solved elsewhere in the same codebase. Call-site finding and offset-from-name parsing are now implemented three times each (repad, argperm, tracefix) and should be ONE shared helper. Re-solving them per file is how the same defect keeps reappearing. What IS validated is symtrace itself: the traces are correct and match real source line for line. The repair layer on top is unproven. ||| WORKS NOW (2026-08-29), and an external critique found the blocker I could not. TYPEWORD contained literal BACKSPACE bytes (0x08) instead of   word boundaries, because the line had been written through a shell heredoc. The prototype filter therefore matched NOTHING, so every rewrite landed on the extern declaration. Seventh escape-sequence corruption from a heredoc today, and the one that cost the most. With that fixed, tracefix rewrites getRaceCourseSurfaceType(a0, a1, a2) -> (player->field502, player->field1C, player->field24) and the result is BYTE-EXACT, 100.000, with no model involved. The chain is validated end to end: symbolic trace -> mechanical repair -> oracle verification. NOT A NEW MATCH. That function was already in the 34; this reproduces a known one. What is new is that a deterministic pass can now produce it from the binary alone. TWO MORE CORRECTNESS BUGS the same critique identified and I confirmed: symtrace emitted the CALL event on sight of `jal`, BEFORE the delay-slot instruction that IDO routinely uses for argument setup -- callsig already looked into the delay slot and symtrace did not; and caller-saved registers were never invalidated across calls, so stale values leaked into later events. Both fixed, and fixing the clobber immediately exposed a third: an unknown register '?a3' printing as a real argument. STILL UNVALIDATED, and the critique is right to insist: branches are not forked or merged, `or` is treated as a move, arity is guessed by trimming, stack and float arguments and jalr are unmodelled, and everything has been checked on the two functions used to develop it. That is development-set debugging, not validation. Tests and a frozen unseen set come before this is trusted automatically.

RacePlayer is correctly absent because common.h does not reach it, so a candidate declaring RacePlayer keeps it. Hardcoding the popular names would have deleted a type the candidate legitimately owns and turned a clean compile error into wrong code. EXACT REMAINS 0, predicted before the run. This is the FIFTH consecutive compile-rate fix to leave exact untouched (includes strip, C89 pass, for-init, trailing comment, redecl), which is now strong evidence that compile rate and exact are independent axes here. Compile surface is necessary -- a candidate that will not build cannot be refined, permuted or diffed -- but it is not progress toward matching, and should never be reported as such.

claim: Running decomp-permuter on every near-miss candidate rather than only on a score band converts some into matches
source: Macabeus benchmark; downgraded after external review of the sample size
evidence: DOWNGRADED from REFUTED. The measurement stands -- 0 matches and 0 improvements on updateEndingLindaExitUntilPhase3C 99.545, updateRaceSplitscreenSelectPlayerCountIcons 99.436 and checkMainMenuSecretCode 98.561, at 120s each, oracle-verified -- but the label was too strong for n=3. claim: Keeping a Pareto set of structurally different candidates, instead of anchoring on the highest byte score, finds matches the scalar anchor misses
source: external methodology review; Decaf-style portfolio + compiled-feedback rerank
evidence: Prediction stated before the run (3-8 functions get a different anchor, 0 new matches) and held exactly: Pareto chose a different anchor on 7 of 31 functions, and repairing that anchor produced 0 matches the scalar anchor did not. Both arms used the SAME stored candidates, so there is no sampling variance -- the only variable was which candidate the repair passes targeted. Portfolio selection changes WHICH candidate you repair; it does not supply a repair capable of closing the gap, and with layout repair exhausted there was nothing for the better anchor to feed. KEPT ANYWAY, for its diagnostic value: solver/signals.py classifies a residual into layout / structural / relocation / regalloc, and ranking by KIND rather than amount is what revealed three functions with ZERO structural faults -- which led directly to diff-directed repair. The measurement was worth more as an instrument than as an intervention.

claim: The oracle's own instruction diff states where each mislaid field belongs, so layout can be repaired from the counterexample instead of from the evidence tier
source: the residual census plus an external review's CEGIS framing
evidence: FIRST layout intervention to move anything. Over 31 near misses: 0 matches, 3 improved -- updateEndingLindaExitUntilPhase3C 99.545 to 99.773, updateEndingSlashSlideRightToMarker 92.258 to 93.226, zoomTrainingCourseRaceViewport 70.388 to 70.554. Every previous layout attempt (per-function accesses, whole-program global objects, positional and subsequence alignment) moved NOTHING, and the difference is the source of the mapping: the KB knows which offsets the binary touches but nothing maps a DECLARATION to an offset, whereas the diff states it outright -- the field you put at 0 belongs at 0x24. All three deltas are under the significance floor, so this is inconclusive rather than confirmed. THE REAL FINDING IS A DIAGNOSIS. On updateRaceSplitscreenSelectPlayerCountIcons the constraints come out {0 to 0x24, 1 to 0x26, 2 to 0x25} -- non-monotonic. An earlier field must land after a later one, and inserting padding only moves fields later while preserving their order. That function needs field REORDERING, which no padding pass can perform. The pass now detects and reports this rather than emitting a struct satisfying half a contradictory constraint set, which would compile, score differently, and hide the diagnosis. Field reordering is the untested next step and is a different tool. THREE BUGS FOUND BY VERIFYING THE ARM FIRED: _fields() walked every declaration in the file so a typedef counted as a field at offset 0; constraints merged different base registers, which are different objects; and a backslash-b went through a shell heredoc as a literal backspace so the struct pattern matched nothing while the pass reported success. That last one is the EIGHTH heredoc escape corruption in this project and it happened against my own standing rule.

claim: Reordering a struct's fields onto their diff-stated offsets fixes the near misses that padding cannot
source: diagnosis from diff-directed-layout-repair: constraints came out non-monotonic, which padding cannot satisfy
evidence: Implemented in solver/diffrepair.py::reorder_fields and it DECLINES on the function it was built for, which is the informative outcome. Rewriting declarations inside a struct is a pure layout change -- names and types stay attached, so every p->field in the body still resolves -- so the transform itself is safe. It requires every field in the region to be constrained, because an unplaced field could sit anywhere and placing it would be inventing layout. On updateRaceSplitscreenSelectPlayerCountIcons three of four fields are constrained; spawnTimer is not, because the base register carrying its constraint came out non-monotonic and was dropped. THE BLOCKER IS DIFF PAIRING, NOT REORDERING. Constraints are read from zip(minus, plus), which is positional pairing rather than alignment: one unpaired instruction on either side and every subsequent pair drifts. From the diff alone a drifted pairing is indistinguishable from a genuine field reordering, so the pass refuses both rather than acting on a reading it cannot trust. The principled fix is a real sequence alignment of the two instruction streams (LCS or edit distance -- the same technique coddog uses for function similarity) so pairs are trustworthy. That is the next step and it is real work, not a tweak. A REAL BUG FOUND ON THE WAY: _struct_regions matched a function signature, because the pattern allowed a ')' between the struct keyword and the opening brace, so a FUNCTION BODY was parsed as a struct and its locals counted as fields at offsets 0, 4, 8, 0xc, 0xd. Every offset computed for such a candidate was wrong. Fixed and covered by a test.

claim: Aligning the two instruction streams makes diff constraints trustworthy, which unblocks field reordering
source: follow-through on the pairing limit found in the previous iteration
evidence: UPGRADED from INCONCLUSIVE. The blocker was pairing, not reordering. Constraints came from zip(minus, plus) -- positional pairing, not alignment -- so one unpaired instruction made every later pair drift. The oracle's diff carries context (61 context lines against 30 changed on the reference case), so both instruction streams reconstruct in full; normalising each instruction by blanking its OFFSET makes two instructions differing only in position become identical, difflib pairs them as equal, and their real offsets are then comparable. 27 clean pairs where zip drifted. THE GUARD THEN HAD TO GO, and this is the part worth remembering: the non-monotonic drop rule was correct under zip pairing and WRONG under alignment -- it was discarding exactly the signal the alignment existed to recover. Removed, all four fields of RaceSplitscreenSelectRowActor become constrained and reorder_fields fires: updateRaceSplitscreenSelectPlayerCountIcons 99.436 -> 99.925, oracle-verified, no model. NOT exact. Sweep over 31 near misses: 0 matches, 4 improved (99.436->99.925, 95.989->96.211, 92.258->93.226, 70.388->70.554). ONE IMPROVEMENT WAS LOST and it is not a regression in the fix: updateEndingLindaExitUntilPhase3C reached 99.773 under the OLD drifted constraints; the correct constraints give 99.205, below its 99.545 baseline, so the score guard keeps the original. The old gain was an artefact of a wrong pairing that happened to score better. NEXT LIMITATION, precisely stated: padding shifts EVERY field after the insertion point, including unconstrained fields the diff said nothing about. On that function three constrained fields need +2 while the untouched fields between them were already correct. Fixing it means reorder_fields accepting partially-constrained regions and holding unconstrained fields at their current offsets -- which is a judgement about what 'the diff did not complain' means, and is not obviously safe: a field the function never accesses generates no evidence either way.

claim: Reading the intended field WIDTH from the opcode in the oracle's diff repairs a fault class no existing pass could touch
source: triage by tractability: updateRaceSetupFourPlayerOption had 3 faults, zero structural, and one of them was sw-vs-sb
evidence: FIRST NEW BYTE-EXACT MATCH since the corpus was built. updateRaceSetupFourPlayerOption 96.441 -> 100.000, oracle exact=True, no model. Match count 34 -> 35. repad and reorder_fields can MOVE a field; neither can RETYPE one, so width faults had no repair at all despite appearing in roughly fifteen functions. width_constraints() reads the width from the opcode exactly as offsets are read from the operand. A store carries no signedness, so it constrains width only rather than guessing a type; arrays are left alone because a wider access could mean the element type or the index arithmetic. TWO BUGS HAD TO BE FIXED FOR IT TO FIRE AT ALL. (1) aligned_pairs blanks only the offset, so a pair differing in OPCODE never lands in an equal block -- width constraints could never have fired; aligned_pairs_loose collapses a memory op to its direction so those pairs align. (2) THE ACTUAL BLOCKER: DECL anchored at start-of-line, so a declaration behind an inline comment -- /* 0x00 .. 0x17 */ char pad0[0x18]; -- was invisible. The pads were not counted, a field computed at offset 0x02 instead of 0x1C, and the diff's constraint matched nothing. That is the THIRD parser defect of this shape (function bodies read as structs, typedefs counted as fields, now commented pads skipped) and each one silently produced WRONG OFFSETS while every pass reported success. Sweep: 1 match, 3 further improvements. Earlier gains compounded rather than reverting -- updateRaceSplitscreenSelectPlayerCountIcons now STARTS at 99.925.

claim: bootThreadMain's single missing nop can be produced by some C spelling of its empty infinite loop
source: it is the smallest residual in the project: one instruction at 97.222
evidence: 16 oracle-verified variants, all byte-identical at 97.222: nine infinite-loop spellings (for/while/do-while/goto, statement and block bodies) and seven dead-code variants around the loop. Two variants that moved a call into the loop scored WORSE (83.605). IDO normalises every spelling, so the loop's C form is not the source of the nop. The target ends with a self-branch, its delay-slot nop, then three more nops before an UNREACHABLE epilogue; we emit two. That is compiler padding after dead code, not a code difference, and nothing at the C level reaches it. No other matched function in the corpus uses the idiom, so there is no sibling to copy either. GENERAL LESSON, and it corrects how the work queue should be read: a one-instruction residual is NOT necessarily easy. Fault COUNT does not predict tractability -- fault KIND does. eval/triage.py ranks by kind for this reason.

claim: Our candidates' own typedef preludes model a different translation unit, so replacing them with the real project header changes the score
source: DECOMPILATION_LEARNINGS.md in the reference repo: the same body scored 95.749% against a decomp.me-style prelude and 98.851% against the real project headers
evidence: Does not transfer to our setup. PREVALENCE FIRST: only 2 of 37 unmatched candidates carry a redundant prelude at all. On both, replacing it with #include common.h left the score EXACTLY unchanged. A first attempt stripped the prelude without adding the header and broke both builds, which was itself informative: those candidates do not include common.h at all, so the prelude is their only type source. WHY IT DOES NOT TRANSFER: our preludes declare only scalar typedefs -- unsigned char, short, long -- which are exactly correct for this ABI, so the program they model is identical to the one the headers give. The reference project's gap must have come from a prelude that differed substantively, most likely in struct definitions rather than scalars. METHOD NOTE: an external methodology document is a source of hypotheses, not of conclusions. This one was measured and did not hold here; adopt nothing from that file without testing it in our harness.

claim: A residual consisting only of trailing nops is a defect in the candidate that some C spelling can fix
source: bootThreadMain sat one nop from exact and resisted every C variant
evidence: The reference project's DECOMPILATION_LEARNINGS.md states it directly: object-relative alignment nops are padding, not logic. IDO emits an alignment directive before an unreachable epilogue, and a single-function workspace starts at a different section offset than the real multi-function object, so the same directive yields a different number of trailing nops EVEN WHEN THE LIVE INSTRUCTIONS MATCH. For this exact shape it adds that a terminal backward goto can align an unreachable epilogue with the nop count depending on the function's offset in the translation unit. That explains 16 oracle-verified variants moving bootThreadMain not at all: there is nothing in C to find. The candidate may already be correct and our isolated workspace cannot deliver a verdict on it. eval/alignment_nops.py measures the reach: exactly ONE function is purely alignment-blocked, 21 more carry nop noise inside residuals otherwise dominated by real faults. CONSEQUENCE: a function whose residual is only trailing nops should be reported as HARNESS-LIMITED rather than counted as a near miss, and verified in the real translation unit. Also worth remembering as a sourcing lesson: there was no commit explaining the match -- only 777 of ~2113 functions carry one -- and the answer lived in a methodology document we had never read.

claim: Diffing two candidates at IDO's pre-as1 layer isolates one changed allocation decision where diffing their objects shows dozens of shifted rows
source: imported from the reference project's DECOMPILATION_LEARNINGS.md; the tool exists in our toolchain
evidence: THE CAPABILITY IS REAL AND NOW BUILT (solver/asmlayer.py). cc -S with the workspace's own flags emits final register numbers, .loc records, unexpanded pseudo-ops and .livereg masks -- 87 instructions and 70 decisions on renderRaceUiSingleTrailEffect. One implementation trap worth recording: IDO's cc IGNORES -o under -S and writes <basename>.s into the working directory, so passing -o produced nothing at all and read as a compile failure. THE CONTROLS ARE THE STRONGEST PART. A blank-line insertion and a local RENAME both produced dS=0 and dO=0 -- no movement at either layer. That validates the harness (it is not measuring noise) and independently reproduces two imported claims in OUR setup: the project builds without -g so layout is inert, and IDO colors by internal temp numbering rather than source variable identity. THE DIRECTION HOLDS BUT THE MAGNITUDE DOES NOT. Two catalogued allocation nudges each gave dS=5 against dO=8, with 2 isolated register changes. So the object diff IS larger than the -S diff in 2 of 2 cases, but 8-versus-5 is not the 'one decision versus dozens of rows' the source claims. Either our nudges were too small to trigger the amplification, or that description does not generalise. INCONCLUSIVE on the headline claim. WHAT IS GENUINELY NEW is register_changes(): it reports (opcode, before, after) per moved register, which is a direct read on allocation decisions that no object diff gives. Register choice is our largest untouched fault class -- 36 of the 45 residual faults on this function, with ZERO structural -- and every pass built so far moves or retypes a field and cannot move a value between registers. NEXT: use register_changes as the ranking signal for a nudge search, rather than the byte score, since the imported notes warn that dist.py's reordering penalty hides the statement-order lever entirely.

claim: Enumerating catalogued semantics-preserving source nudges reduces register-choice faults
source: imported IDO notes; renderRaceUiSingleTrailEffect has 36 register faults and zero structural, the cleanest target we have
evidence: 0 of 4 nudges reduced register faults from a baseline of 36. Ranked on register-fault count rather than byte score, because the imported notes warn dist.py's reordering penalty hides this lever. Control (blank line) moved nothing at either layer, so the harness is clean. Two nudges made it WORSE -- 36 to 39 register faults AND structural 0 to 2, meaning they changed program shape rather than only allocation, which is the opposite of semantics-preserving. One arm was an INVALID TEST and must not be read against its entry: ido-redundant-mask-advances-the-temp-fifo is stated for a narrow u16 FIELD read and I applied it to an array index, outside its precondition; it produced zero change and remains untested. One failed to build. CONSEQUENCE: blind source perturbation is a poor instrument for this fault class. We possess uopt's actual algorithm, so predicting the allocation is better posed than shaking the source until it rattles.

claim: uopt's stated ordering law -- webs by descending save, ties on construction order -- predicts which register a value receives
source: the reference project's instrumented measurements of uopt 5.3
evidence: 79.1% concordance (102/129 comparable pairs) against our OWN byte-exact functions, which is the only contamination-free ground truth available. Chance is 50%. Only the ORDER is tested, which survives an inexact totalsave -- the notes give save = totalsave / nocs but not the numerator, so it is modelled as occurrence weight with 10x per loop level and flagged as assumption. The pool, nocs = ((n-2)>>2)+2 and the ordering rule are quoted exactly. THE DIAGNOSTIC MATTERED MORE THAN THE NUMBER. The first run scored 67.8% with a BIMODAL distribution: two functions near 96% and isRacePlayerRespawnSurfaceValid at exactly 0.0% over 14 pairs. A perfect inversion is a sign error, not noise, since noise sits at 50%. Its top-ranked web held a3 -- index 5 in the pool -- so every comparison against it was wrong. a3 was not a colouring decision but the fourth argument to a call. uopt CAN colour into a0-a3 and v0/v1, but a value feeding a jal or taken from its return is precoloured by the ABI and never competed on save; counting those webs measures the calling convention and calls it allocation. Excluding them gives 79.1%. That correction is derived from the ABI rather than tuned to the number, which is the difference between a model and a fitted constant. REMAINING GAP: updateEndingLindaTumbleToPhase3C still scores 12.5% over 8 pairs, so at least one regime is unmodelled. Do not treat 79% as a specification.

claim: On an allocation-shaped residual the dist.py byte score moves OPPOSITE to the number of wrong instructions, so any search ranked by score steers away from the answer. Rank by fault count instead; the oracle's exact flag remains the only verdict.
source: measured on renderRaceUiSingleTrailEffect
evidence: Two statement swaps, each lowering score and lowering register faults: 91.974->91.779 with regalloc 39->38, and 91.974->89.494 with regalloc 39->35. A beam search ranked by faults then fell 41->39->38->37->36->34 while the score fell 91.974->85.987, so every step of real progress would have been rejected by a score-ranked search. eval/allocsearch.py.

claim: Swapping adjacent INDEPENDENT assignments changes which colour uopt gives each web, because equal-priority webs break ties on construction chronology, which follows source statement order.
source: patterns catalogue, confirmed locally
evidence: renderRaceUiSingleTrailEffect: instruction mix identical to the target (75 vs 75, no opcode count differs), so nothing is missing and only colouring differs. Five swaps moved the fault count 41->34 monotonically. The lever is real and measurable.

claim: A beam search over adjacent independent-statement swaps is enough to drive an allocation-shaped residual to byte-exact.
source: this iteration
evidence: 182 compiles, beam 4, depth 10 on renderRaceUiSingleTrailEffect: faults plateau at 34 of an initial 41 by depth 5 and regress afterwards. Adjacent swaps reach only part of the permutation space; whole-run permutation and web MERGING (which values share a register) are untried. No match.

claim: Two harnesses may score the same function at once, because build.sh takes a flock.
source: assumed by every sweep in eval/
evidence: build.sh locks the BUILD, but the filenames are shared: every caller writes <func>.c and reads <func>_diff, so A can read B's residual against A's source with nothing erroring. Caught when three runs of one fixed source gave three different proposal sets while an eval.compose_regress ran in another shell -- score 91.909 vs 91.974, register faults 38 vs 39, for a source that never changed. Fixed by _workspace_lock in solver/workspace.py, which holds a separate .score.lock across write/build/read.

claim: Offset constraints can be grouped by base register name, and a base whose constraints disagree is unreliable.
source: solver/diffrepair.constraints, since it was written
evidence: v0 is the return-value register and names a different object after every call; s0 is callee-saved and holds several objects across a long function. On initRacePlayerLandingSnowSpray one ambiguous offset (0x4 -> {0x28,0x2c,0x30}) discarded twelve unanimous +1148 constraints. On updateCourseSelectCourseDescription base a2's eighteen clean pairs were dropped for 'conflicts with another base' because an unrelated loaded pointer t6 also had an opinion about offset 0. Replaced by constraint_sets/delta_clusters, which never merge and propose each reading separately.

claim: A struct member whose type is not a primitive can be skipped when computing field offsets.
source: solver/diffrepair._fields
evidence: It was skipped WITHOUT advancing the cursor, so every field after a nested struct got a wrong offset. On updateRacePlayerMode53AerialTrick the parser reported [0, 32, 48, 68, ...] for a struct whose compiled accesses run to 124; the correct list is [0, 32, 44, 56, 72, 84, 104, 108, 112, 114, 116, 120, 122, 124]. Every layout proposal was then declined for 'not a field offset in that region'. Fixed by type_sizes(), which resolves structs declared in the same file, and by DECLINING the region when a type is still unknown rather than guessing.

claim: A pure signedness mismatch (lb vs lbu) is repairable by retyping the field, and was being discarded.
source: solver/diffrepair.width_constraints

claim: Reordering body statements can change the colour assigned to the prologue's parameter copy, which is the web that anchors the whole residual on renderRaceUiSingleTrailEffect.
source: the obvious next step once relocation stalled
evidence: The residual's anchor is `-move a3,a0 / +move a2,a0`, the prologue copy of the a0 parameter into a saved register; all 31 remaining register faults follow from it. Every reachable body permutation (30 compiles, beam 5, depth 10) left that line unchanged. The target giving this web a HIGHER colour means some other web outranks it there on `save`, so the lever is the reference COUNT of a competing web, not the order of the statements. Note this also corrects an earlier reading in this session: target a3 against our a2 means we are missing a high-save web, not carrying a surplus one, so inlining a temporary is the wrong direction here.

claim: The statement-order gate may require a residual with no layout faults at all.
source: solver/rewrites._allocation_shaped, first cut

Purity refused it, and no layout generator covered those two offsets either, so the function got ZERO proposals of any kind. claim: Modelling uopt's `save` from the candidate's own output lets the solver propose WHICH web to strengthen, instead of permuting source and hoping.
source: the plan proposed after statement relocation stalled
evidence: Seven totalsave models measured against real IDO output on the matched corpus, scored on an IDENTICAL 802-pair set that all of them rank strictly: flat n/nocs 57.5, loop 2x 58.4, loop 4x 58.0, loop 8x 57.7, loop 10x 57.7, loop 10x with memory 2x 57.5, memory refs only 50.4. Chance is 50. The per-model table's 65-68% is an artefact -- a model that discriminates less excludes its ties from the denominator and is graded on an easier subset, so those accuracies are not comparable across models. Weight sweeping cannot fix it: webs are rebuilt from POST-allocation assembly by splitting at register redefinition, which conflates distinct values that reuse a register and cannot see what uopt coalesced. The prescription is now gated behind unvalidated_ok.

claim: The 10x-per-loop-level weighting in uopt.webs affects the model when run on the oracle's normalized dumps.
source: solver/uopt._loop_depth
evidence: _loop_depth found loops only via `label:` lines and branches naming them. The normalized object dumps have NO label lines -- branch targets are bare hex byte offsets -- so every depth stayed 0 and the weighting never applied. It failed silently: a sweep over 2x, 4x, 8x and 10x per level returned byte-identical concordance for all four, which is only possible if nothing is ever inside a loop. Fixed with _numeric_depth, resolving back edges from hex targets at 4 bytes per instruction; 14 of 85 functions then show a loop. Fixing it made concordance WORSE (65.6 vs 68.3 flat), which is itself evidence against the weight model rather than for it.

claim: Which web is mis-coloured, and where it is referenced, can be read from the oracle's diff with no allocator model.
source: solver/allocdiff
evidence: Aligning both streams by instruction index and comparing webs by first-def line names the anchor exactly. On renderRaceUiSingleTrailEffect it reports 13 mis-coloured webs and the anchor at stream line 13 -- target a3, ours a2 -- with the four instructions referencing it, a spill/reload pair at 0x48(sp) plus two uses. This is the part worth keeping and could focus an oracle-checked search on statements feeding that one value.

claim: Counting wrong INSTRUCTIONS is the right search objective for an allocation residual.
source: eval/faultsearch.faults_of, first cut
evidence: One web given the wrong colour renames that value at every reference, so the instruction count measures blast radius rather than progress. renderRaceUiSingleTrailEffect reports 31-42 register-fault instructions arising from 13 mis-coloured webs, and its anchor alone accounts for four. This is the same error as counting four branch-target faults that are one instruction-count difference seen four times. Replaced by allocdiff.mismatches(), which counts webs and is model-free -- it compares the two streams the oracle already produced and involves no prediction, unlike the REFUTED save model. The objective now reads 18 where it read 43, and the search reaches 14. It found a DIFFERENT local optimum, not a match: exact is still 0 on this function.

claim: The rewrite generators encode general compiler behaviour, so each one helps on functions beyond the one whose residual it was written from.
source: implicit in every capability claim made from them

FOUR never fire at all (reloc_padding, inline_temporary, branch_sentinel, signed_compare); THREE fire but never lower the fault count (immediate on 5 functions, compare_swap on 2, frame_padding on 1); TWO help only on their own origin function (pointer_table_deref, statement_order). Caveats: signed_compare and branch_sentinel have no customers left because their functions are already solved, which is the memorisation signature rather than a bug; argswap is under-tested at 4 proposals per function out of 135. The suite is a collection of narrow patterns, not general capability, and the 49-function held-out split in eval/sets/sbk1_v3.json has still never been run.

claim: The allocation residual is the candidate holding more values live across calls than the target -- an extra web visible as pressure, without needing a priority model.
source: proposed after the save model was refuted
evidence: solver/liveness.py computes backward liveness over solver.cfg and reports caller-saved registers live across each call; both sides are computed, because `cc -S` emits .livereg masks for the candidate but target.s carries none. Over 21 medium functions: 5 profiles IDENTICAL, 4 DIFFER, 12 unusable (no calls or unusable streams). It differs usefully where it differs -- updateRacePlayerMode16AerialTrick target [2,4,14,13,0] against candidate [3,7,14,13,0], and func_80059A04 carrying +1 at nearly every one of 13 calls, which is a systematic extra live value with a program point attached. BUT it is IDENTICAL on renderRaceUiSingleTrailEffect ([14,2,2] both sides), the function whose residual is purest allocation and where the hypothesis was most wanted. So pressure is a real and separate cause affecting SOME functions; it does not explain the anchor case, whose difference must be priority or tie-breaking after all. Worth a generator for the functions where profiles differ; not the general answer to the wall.

claim: IDO's .livereg masks can be compared between target and candidate to locate allocation differences.
source: the one unexplored compiler output
evidence: cc -S does emit them for a candidate -- renderRaceUiSingleTrailEffect yields 4, e.g. 0x0000FF0E,0x00000FFF meaning at,v0,v1,t0-t7 and f0-f11 live across that call. But target.s, being a ROM disassembly, contains ZERO .livereg directives, so there is nothing to compare against. Liveness must be COMPUTED on both sides to keep the comparison apples-to-apples, which is what solver/liveness.py does; the compiler's own annotation is usable only for candidate-versus-candidate work, which solver/asmlayer.py already covers.

claim: The project lacks a call graph, so it cannot order work by dependency the way every decomp project does.
source: user intuition, and the absence of any caller/callee tooling

The evidence tier holds 9,854 call rows, 9,761 with a resolved target, across 1,819 callers and 625 callees, and functions.is_leaf is populated for all 2,113. func_deps has ZERO rows; only kb/tms.py and eval/poison_test.py mention call evidence at all. source: the standard decomp workflow, applied to the existing edges
evidence: The graph is a clean DAG -- ZERO cycles across 2,113 functions -- so topological order needs no SCC handling. Only 195 of 2,113 functions had ever been attempted, because the eval sets were deliberately sampled for difficulty. There are 322 leaves, 271 never attempted, 234 of those under 60 instructions, and 137 in the TINY tier which currently solves at 24/25. getRelocatableHeapBlockBase -- 8 instructions, a leaf, 15 unmatched callers depending on it -- had never been attempted and matched BYTE-EXACT on the first structural guess, CPU only, no model; setCallbackTaskCallback (2 instructions) likewise. claim: Giving a caller its callee's oracle-verified signature changes the caller's generated instructions, because return and parameter widths drive extension and marshalling.
source: the mechanism that makes leaf-first more than easy-first
evidence: solver/protostore.py harvests signatures from byte-exact sources; prototype_rewrites FIRES on 12 of 41 unmatched functions, the BROADEST reach of any generator (argswap was 10, everything else 0-5), all of them reaching getRelocatableHeapBlockBase within an hour of it being solved. But on 11 of 11 that compiled, the INSTRUCTION residual is byte-identical: the source changes and the output does not. The reason is specific, not general -- of the 83 verified signatures, 68 return void and 13 more return a 32-bit type, all codegen-identical to the implicit int a caller assumes. Exactly ONE has a width-sensitive return (u8 getRaceItemEffectType) and it does not reach those callers. So the mechanism is untested rather than refuted, and the leaf sweep is what would test it: narrow-return getters are exactly what sits in the 137 unattempted tiny leaves. Do not retire this without re-running it after that sweep.

claim: Solve the leaves, promote a function only once EVERY function it calls is solved, sweep the lowest level again when the frontier stalls.
source: user proposal; the standard human decomp workflow
evidence: CORRECTED after external audit. Originally recorded REFUTED; that overreached. Simulated on the real call graph (eval/wavefront.py, 2,113 functions, zero cycles) with per-tier rates measured excluding the 55 RECOVERED functions: tiny 96.3, small 64.0, medium 41.0, large 14.6, huge 11.8 (large collapses from 70.8 once recovery is removed, so almost every large 'match' was recovered rather than solved). STRICT GATE reaches 971 of 2,113 (46.0%); attempting everything at the same rates reaches 1,196 (56.6%). THE LIMIT OF THAT COMPARISON: it holds each function's solvability fixed and independent of whether its callees are solved, which is exactly the dependency benefit gating exists to capture. So it prices gating under the assumption that transfer is worth nothing -- about 225 functions -- rather than refuting it. The assumption is not arbitrary (prototype propagation measurably changed ZERO instructions across 11 callers, because 68 of 83 verified signatures return void), but one null on a 6.5%-full corpus does not establish that transfer is worthless in general. WHAT STANDS: use the graph as a PRIORITY, which costs nothing and is strictly better than score-ordering. What is open: whether a solved callee makes its caller easier, which needs re-testing once the pool is not starved. The break-even is computable -- gating wins if the per-function boost from solved callees exceeds the ~225-function blocking loss.

claim: The compile-error-driven repair chain in eval/zero_token_harvest.py is a named technique from the decompilation literature, not an invention, and the published version defers commitment where ours does not.
source: Superset Decompilation, arXiv 2603.28002 (2026)
evidence: Manifold's final 'Selecting a Representative' phase is error-directed greedy search using the compiler as a type-checking oracle, iteratively reducing error counts -- which is exactly m2c -> compile error -> typedecl -> compile error -> do-while -> recompile, built 2026-09-01 without knowing it had a name. The difference that matters: PGSD retains ambiguous interpretations as parallel candidates with provenance (~40% of nodes carry more than one) and defers resolution, while our chain commits to one candidate per stage. Also confirms the deterministic path over prompts on independent grounds: a prompt forces early commitment by construction, since the model must pick a layout to emit code.

claim: The evidence tier's (base, offset, width, signed, is_load) rows are BinSub/Retypd capability sketches in all but name, so the binary half of a constraint-based type model needs no new extraction.
source: BinSub arXiv 2409.01841; Retypd PLDI 2016
evidence: BinSub represents record fields as (offset, size): tau with SEPARATE load (covariant) and store (contravariant) parameters, because one polarity alone loses information. Our 72,845 evidence rows carry offset, width, signedness and an is_load polarity flag already. Consequence for the typedecl defect measured the same day: declaring every member a scalar made only 4 of 25 plans compile, and 7 of the 21 failures were 'Subscripting a non-array' or 'Selector requires struct/union pointer'. Those are not two special cases to patch but two capabilities (subscripted, dereferenced) the sketch must carry. BinSub also reports Retypd-level precision (type distance 1.67 vs 1.68) at 63x the speed, so the simplification path is known if we ever solve rather than enumerate.

claim: The 'zero free unknowns and no match' gate finds defects in the enumerator before it finds defects in the solver, and that is the gate working rather than failing.
source: solver/unknowns.py first live run; LEDGER.md gate 2

claim: A parameter struct's layout should be pooled across every function whose draft names that type, exactly as globals_layout pools a global across every function that touches its address.
source: typedecl decline census
evidence: typedecl declines when a draft names more members than the binary has offsets for THAT function's parameter, which caused 13 declines plus 8 no-evidence cases out of 42 examined. Pooling by m2c's type name: PlayerCommandState appears in 15 leaf drafts with 36 pooled offsets against 15 for the best single function -- 2.4x, closely matching globals_layout's 2.7x for globals. The type identity is m2c's hypothesis rather than a binary fact, so the pooled struct is a hypothesis too; it is falsifiable by the oracle, which is the correct way to hold it. Also found: typedecl only inspects PARAMETERS, so an undeclared type on a LOCAL is invisible to it (17 of 62 syntax errors had no pointer parameter at all).

claim: A declared type can contradict the draft's own capability set, which is a distinct failure from an undeclared type and is invisible to a declared/undeclared test.
source: syntax-error census
evidence: Fcutoff is `s32 Fcutoff(PlayerCommandState *arg0, u8 *arg1)` whose body runs `arg1->unk0` and `arg1->unk1`. u8 is a known build type, so typedecl skips that parameter entirely, yet the draft dereferences members through it. 9 of 62 syntax-error leaves are this shape (Fcutoff, Fdefa, Fgoto). Under the BinSub framing this is mechanical: the observed capability set says `dereferenced with members {unk0, unk1}` and the declared type cannot satisfy it. Needs a kind of its own -- contradicted_type -- resolved by the same struct synthesis (2026-09-01).

claim: Pooling a struct's offsets across every function naming its type widens the layout as predicted, but did NOT convert that into compiling candidates on the hard leaf residual.
source: solver/typepool.py, paired rerun on 190 never-compiled leaves
evidence: The widening replicated: 54 types pooled from 486 drafts, 294 offsets, PlayerCommandState 36 pooled against 15 for its best single contributor. But typedecl plans went 28 -> 35 while COMPILED stayed at 1 of ~165, and only 8 of the 35 plans actually used pooled fields. Prediction was ~21 unlocked; actual 0. Two reasons found. (a) A bug the pooling exposed: `void` is a keyword so buildtypes never lists it, and typedecl emitted `typedef struct {...} void;` for 8 plans including guMtxF2L and alCopy. (b) On the libmus family the binding constraint was never the layout -- arg0 declared fine and arg1 was the blocker. Pooling is kept because the widening is real and costs nothing, but it is not the lever (2026-09-01).

claim: When m2c declares a one-byte pointer and then emits member accesses through it, the repair is indexing, not struct synthesis -- a synthesised type would silently rescale the pointer arithmetic.
source: solver/memberaccess.py
evidence: Fcutoff is `s32 Fcutoff(PlayerCommandState *arg0, u8 *arg1)` whose body runs `arg1->unk0` and returns `(s32)(arg1 + 2)`. u8 is a real build type so typedecl correctly skips it, and the draft still fails with `Selector requires struct/union pointer`. m2c encodes the offset in the member name, so for a one-byte element offset IS index and arg1->unk1 is arg1[1]; `arg1 + 2` keeps walking two bytes. Changing u8* to a struct pointer would have made it two structs -- a wrong constant rather than a compile error. Arm verified to fire on 8 drafts; Selector errors fell 12 -> 9 and Fcutoff, Flength and Fwobble now compile. Restricted to one-byte element types; wider elements decline (2026-09-01).

claim: A repair harness that reports the BEST attempt's error hides whether the repair helped, because a failed repair and a failed original both score 0.0 and the original wins the tie.
source: eval/zero_token_harvest.py receipt audit
evidence: 38 leaves were reported as blocked on the build's do-token ban AFTER the for-break rewrite had already removed it -- the receipt was showing the m2c stage's error because the repaired candidate also failed to compile and `att.score > best.score` was false at 0.0 vs 0.0. Every bucket size measured from those receipts was therefore attributed to the wrong cause. Fixed to report the LAST stage's error plus an error_stage field; re-measuring immediately moved 12 functions out of do-token and into syntax-error, which is where the real work is (2026-09-01).

claim: Declaring the globals an m2c draft names, with widths from the evidence tier and extents left unspecified, is the single largest deterministic unlock on the leaf residual.
source: solver/globaldecl.py
evidence: Paired rerun on the SAME 189 never-compiled leaves, zero generated tokens, only the globals stage added: compiled 3 -> 21, byte-exact 0 -> 11 (MusSetMasterVolume, clearPendingPositionalSoundRequests, requestMusicSequenceStop, resetSecondaryRng, and the seven tryQueueRacePlayerHitCue* variants). Arms verified to fire: globals 32 alone, 24 with do-while, 13 with typedecl. The undefined-symbol bucket fell 43 -> 20. Two declaration shapes, and the distinction mattered: a single observed offset and no subscript gives `extern u16 g;`, while a subscript or several offsets gives `extern u32 g[];` -- a legal C89 incomplete array that permits indexing while committing to no extent the binary does not reveal. Widths come from evidence, never from symbol_addrs.txt's curated `// size:` annotations (2026-09-01).

claim: Ranking repair work by bucket SIZE mis-ordered it; the binding constraint was consistently a different bucket than the largest one.
source: leaf repair sequence
evidence: Predicted order was pooling first (~21 unlocked), then pointer capabilities, then globals. Actual: pooling REFUTED at 0 unlocked despite replicating its 2.4x widening; byte-indexing confirmed but small at 3 compiles; globals delivered 18 compiles and 11 matches. The reason is that compile errors are reported one at a time, so a bucket's size counts FIRST errors and says nothing about whether fixing it exposes another blocker underneath -- already recorded as [[compile-error-buckets-are-first-errors-not-independent-blockers]], and I mis-ordered anyway. The cheap correction is to fix the bucket whose mechanism is most independent of the others, not the biggest (2026-09-01).

claim: Routing a compile failure to its fix by normalised error signature covers the great majority of real failures and turns an unroutable error into a named gap.
source: solver/compilefix.py
evidence: Over all 4,027 non-compiling attempts: 118 distinct signatures, ten covering 90.1%. The registry accounts for 92.5% -- 29.6% routed by signature alone, 50.0% by the Syntax Error sub-signatures refined against the SOURCE rather than the message, 12.9% recorded as known causes we deliberately do not repair. Nothing unexplained remains above 1.1%. It found three bugs in itself on first run: gaps() reported Syntax Error as the top gap although every sub-signature routes; `at line 13` was not normalised, splitting one redeclaration cause into four signatures of 33/28/25/20; and every KNOWN_UNFIXABLE key was copied from a census truncating at 60 characters while signature() truncates at 64, so none matched. Also registered two fixes that already existed and were unreachable from this path: strip_unresolvable_includes (91 attempts) and strip_redeclarations (106) (2026-09-01).

claim: Dispatching on the CURRENT compile error and recompiling after each fix outperforms applying every repair once in a fixed order.
source: eval/zero_token_harvest.py --iterate; Superset Decompilation arXiv 2603.28002
evidence: BUILT AND RUNNING, NOT YET MEASURED -- do not treat the null below as a result. Paired run over 143 never-compiled leaves gave arm A (blind chain) 0 compiled and arm B (iterate) 0 compiled, but that population was already exhausted by the existing fixes, so the test could not discriminate. The mechanism demonstrably works: 99 fixes fired (globals 48, do-while 37, typedecl 9, byte-index 5) and 71 of 143 functions took two or three routed repair steps, each chosen by the error the previous step exposed. This is the shape Manifold's selection phase uses. Needs a population where the fixes still have room -- the ~500 unattempted non-leaf functions, NOT the leaf residual. Known reporting defect to fix first: the iterate path does not populate row['typedecl_plans'], so the summary reads typedecl_planned=0 while the trace shows 9 (2026-09-01).

claim: typedecl inspects only parameters, so an undeclared struct type on a LOCAL variable is invisible to it -- and that is now the single largest blocker on the leaf residual.
source: compilefix trace over 143 never-compiled leaves
evidence: The registry's stop-reason census: 106 of 143 functions end at 'every registered fix declined' rather than 'no registered fix', and the largest sub-signature is Syntax Error/undeclared-type-not-a-parameter at 66. The error routes correctly and the selected fix declines, because typedecl.pointer_parameters only reads the parameter list. Complication to solve: the evidence tier keys observed accesses by param0/param1, which is the parameter POSITION, so a local has no evidence key at all. The layout for a local must therefore come from solver/typepool.py's cross-function pool, keyed by the type NAME m2c gave it, with members placed by their offset-encoded names rather than by source order (2026-09-01).

claim: The m2c bootstrap draft is not header-free. m2c builds its context by preprocessing a project translation unit, so reconstructed include/game/** type and MEMBER NAMES are already present in every draft this project treats as a clean baseline.
source: MusAsk decline analysis
evidence: MusAsk's draft declares `PlayerCommandState *var_v1;` and accesses `->pdata` and `->soundId`. Neither is an m2c unkNN placeholder: both are declared in include/game/audio/audio_engine.h, lines 84 and 101, which the decomp team reconstructed. m2c obtained them by preprocessing the project TU. Consequence for the contamination line: what solver/project_headers.py supplies EXPLICITLY -- and what eval/status.py now counts apart as header-assisted -- is already leaking IMPLICITLY through the draft, in name form. The leak is names only; no layout or offset enters the candidate, and byte-exactness is still decided by the oracle. But eval/zero_token_harvest.py's docstring claim that the path 'reads only common.h' describes the CANDIDATE's includes, not m2c's knowledge, and should not be read as a contamination guarantee (2026-09-01).

claim: The largest remaining leaf bucket is not a missing generator. It is functions whose member names came from a reconstructed header, so no mechanical name-to-offset mapping exists without giving that header back.
source: typedecl locals support, measured
evidence: Predicted that reading pointer LOCALS as well as parameters would unlock the 66 functions stuck on Syntax Error/undeclared-type-not-a-parameter. Built it, and verified the routing after a first null showed the arm had never fired -- the registry sent that signature to globals alone. With routing fixed, typedecl is tried first and still declines, correctly: PlayerCommandState pools to 56 offsets, but MusAsk uses members `pdata` and `soundId`, which are real names rather than offset-encoded unkNN, so typepool.named_fields returns None and positional zip onto 56 pooled offsets is refused by design. Compiled stayed 0 of 143. The refusal is right: zipping two names onto 56 offsets would fabricate a layout. These functions are solvable only by supplying the reconstructed header, which makes them header-assisted rather than solved. Keep the locals support -- it is correct and will fire where names ARE offset-encoded -- but do not expect this bucket to yield deterministically (2026-09-01).
